name: Low-Budget Black-Box Optimization Benchmark
description:
Machine learning has invaded various domains of computer science, including black-box optimization. Recent research is particularly concerned with Bayesian Optimization and/or Monte Carlo Tree Search.
However, the experiments are usually performed on rather small benchmarks and there are visible issues in the experimental setup, such as poor initialization of baselines, overfitting by specifying hyperparameters specifically for each test function, and low statistical significance. In addition, the interface is sometimes very problem-specific and has more impact on the results than the algorithm itself.
We compare several black-box optimization tools from the machine learning world and benchmark them on the classical BBOB benchmark, which is well known in the black-box optimization field, and on Direct Policy Search for OpenAI Gym. In particular, the benchmarks in this work include randomization of the optimum: BBOB considers 15 random instances per test function and dimension, i.e., 24 functions $\times$ 6 dimensionalities $\times$ 15 random instances $=2160$ cases. For OpenAI Gym, we consider tiny and larger neural networks, on a total number of 13 problems $\times$ 8 budgets $\times$ 10 repetitions $=1040$ and 18 problems $\times$ 8 budgets $\times$ 10 repetitions $=1440$ instances, respectively.
evaluation_method: best_found_value / regret (often reported as expected running time (ERT) to reach target or final objective value); for policy search also average return
general_score_metric: best_found_value / regret (ERT on BBOB); average return for policy-search tasks
reputation: Well-known within the black-box optimization research community (BBOB is a standard), but less widely used across broader ML benchmarks.
notes: Non-LLM benchmark; randomized instances and multiple budgets; computationally intensive; results sensitive to initialization and hyperparameter tuning; risk of overfitting algorithms to the specific test functions.
